title: The impact understanding of exosome therapy in COVID-19 and preparations for the future approaches in dealing with infec

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 4 is captioned 'Comparing cytokine levels after exosome treatment using paired T-test' and its legend defines 'SD, Standard deviation; 95% CI, 95% Confidence interval; t, test statistic, Cohen's d: effect size...'. However, the actual table reports 'Median ± IQR', 'Z', 'P-value', and 'r' for each cytokine/condition — i.e., Wilcoxon signed-rank statistics, not paired t-test statistics (no means/SD, t-values, CIs, or Cohen's d appear anywhere in the table). The reported values and footnote markers (a/b/c/d referring to 'based on negative/positive ranks') are identical in structure to the following Table 5, which is explicitly described as the Wilcoxon test table. This shows Table 4's caption does not match its content, i.e., the table shown is actually a Wilcoxon table mislabeled as a paired t-test table.

The text states: 'Various doses of 10 µg/ml, 20 µg/ml, 40 µg/ml, and 60 µg/ml were evaluated for this purpose... a dose of 40 µg/mL (the highest dose) was selected as the optimal dose.' This is self-contradictory: 60 µg/ml was explicitly listed as one of the tested doses and is numerically higher than 40 µg/ml, so 40 µg/ml cannot be described as 'the highest dose' tested.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 4 / Table 5 vs. Abstract and Results text
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The study explicitly states the cytokines evaluated were 'TNF-α, IL-6, IL-17, and IFN-γ' (Abstract, Keywords) and reports a specific p-value for TNF-α (0.055) in the exosome+virus condition in the Results text. However, Table 4 (and the referenced Table 5) only contain rows for IL-6, IFN-γ, and IL-17 — TNF-α is completely absent from the table despite being one of the four primary outcome cytokines and despite the text discussing TNF-α statistics that should be supported by this table.

The abstract concludes: 'These findings underscore the potential safety and efficacy of exosomes as a therapeutic strategy for COVID-19.' However, the study only performed an in vitro cytokine-release assay on PBMCs from n=5 patients and n=5 healthy controls; no actual exosome administration to patients, no adverse event monitoring, and no clinical outcome assessment were performed. Claims of 'safety' and 'efficacy… as a therapeutic strategy' are not supported by this very limited ex vivo cytokine assay and represent an overstatement of the evidence presented.

The abstract describes 'five COVID-19 patients in the intensive care unit, who were subjected to both inactivated SARS-CoV-2 and exosome therapy,' which implies that patients themselves received exosome therapy as a clinical intervention. However, the actual methodology (as later clarified: 'This study aimed to explore the use of exosomes derived from hUC-MSCs to decrease inflammation in COVID-19 patients in a laboratory setting') involved exposing isolated PBMCs ex vivo to inactivated virus and/or exosomes in culture, not administering exosome therapy to the patients. This creates a misleading impression of an in vivo therapeutic intervention when the actual experiment was an in vitro PBMC stimulation assay.
